DIVORCE COURT FOR ONTARIO Mr. WILLIAM IRVINE (Wetaskiwin): Mr. Speaker, on March 12 I gave notice of motion, which appears upon the votes and proceedings for that date and which I desire to move now, seconded by Mr. Kellner. That notice of motion reads:
That Bill No. 20, an act to provide in the province of Ontario for the dissolution and annulment of mariage, be read a second time on Tuesday, the 18th of March, instant.
I have no desire to debate this motion at any great length because I would prefer to trust the issue to the disposition of the house. Hon. members will realize that the rules of the house will not permit a discussion on the merits of the bill itself so the only matter now before the house is whether or not the bill shall be read a second time.
Since this motion virtually asks parliament to consider a bill which already has been dealt with, I must state without undue elaboration my reasons which I hope will be considered adequate.
As hon. members are aware, Bill No. 20 provides in effect for the establishment of divorce courts in the province of Ontario, It was read a second time on Tuesday, March 11, during the hour for private bills. The result
Divorce Court for Ontario

of the vote upon that occasion was unsatisfactory ; I do not mean that it was unsatisfactory to myself or to hon. members who like myself were interested in the success of the bill, but it was unsatisfactory to the house and I think I am safe in saying, from what I have read since, that it was unsatisfactory to the country.
Bill No. 20 has been very contentious, having been moved in the house for several years. It has been very contentious in parliament and outside of parliament; it threatens to arouse latent religious animosities. Therefore I submit it was and is desirable that parliament should speak in no uncertain voice in regard to it. The vote should be decisive, but unfortunately on the 11th instant the vote was not decisive. There was registered against the bill a majority of one. A majority of one would be decisive under ordinary circumstances. If, for instance, there had been as many hon. members present on that occasion as we have in the house to-day, a majority of one would have been as decisive as a majority of several, but on that occasion there were present only 157 members out of 245. I do not wish to reflect on hon. members who were not present. Let me draw the attention of the house to a set of circumstances which combined to produce the unsatisfactory result which the motion before us now seeks to correct. It was anticipated that the bill would give rise to a protracted discussion; it was reasonable to expect that from previous experiences. The bill had been before the house in the private bills' hour for only one night prior to the vote to which I refer, so that hon. members did not expect a vote to come at that time. I know I did not expect a vote myself and I have been interested in the bill. It happened that the discussion terminated suddenly, shortly after the opening of the sitting at eight o'clock, with the result that many hon. members had not time to get back to the house. In fact I know that perhaps about a score of members arrived in the lobbies after the question had been put and they were therefore, by the rules of the house precluded from voting. This fact accounted in a large measure for the small vote.
Another consideration which I offer to the house is that a slight error was made by the clerks in counting the vote. In the house we of course paid very little attention to that. The error did not alter the result at the moment, but it did increase the dissatisfaction both in the house and outside of it.

Another thing we should take note of in this connection is that there was a misunderstanding as to the recognition of pairs. I do not again wish to suggest that any hon. member broke faith designedly, but the fact remains that certain hon. members who were away on urgent business and had their pairs arranged, assuming that the pairs would be recognized under all circumstances, were very much dismayed and dissatisfied to discover that the pairs were broken. In fact, I think the only pair recognized was that by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) who was paired with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). These circumstances which I have enumerated may not be regarded by hon. members as constituting a sufficient reason for voting again for the second reading of the bill to-day, but I will offer no others to the house.
I hope the majority of the house, in view of all the circumstances, are as dissatisfied with the vote as I am, and also appreciate the desirability of having a decisive vote on the issue. So I ask that parliament speak with decision on this matter. If that should result in the defeat of the bill, then those interested in the issue can turn their efforts in another direction. I appeal to the fairness and good judgment of the house. This is not a party issue. So far as I know, neither the government nor the opposition have compromised their following in any way on this matter. The only obligation that we have is as individuals to ourselves and to the issue before us, and so I hope every member will consider the question. I know, as has occurred in other instances, religious convictions and sentiments enter into a vote of this kind. I have every respect for the sincerity of hon. members, whether they be Catholic or Protestant, who vote in accordance with their convictions; but let us vote anyway; let us have a decisive vote on this matter. All I ask is for the voice of parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I am free to admit that my hon. friend has the right to move this motion for the second reading of this bill at another date, although it is most unusual that this should be done in the house. Apparently under the authority of parliamentary writers, the motion that was defeated the other day was "that the bill be now read a second time," and the defeat of that motion would not preclude a motion like the one which is presented to-day. But if technically my hon. friend has the right to move to reconsider the division that was taken the

Divorce Court for Ontario
other day, I do not think this should be countenanced by the house, as io do so would, I think, be creating a dangerous precedent. I venture to say -that no hon. member who voted the other evening either for or against the second reading of the bill, had any misconception about his vote. They all thought they were voting either for or against the principle of the bill and never had in mind the idea that they were voting simply whether the second reading should be given that night or the following day or any other day. As I said, this would be creating a very bad precedent and would be contrary to the well established practice in parliament that when a decision is reached on a question during the session it cannot be brought up again at some other time during the same session. Under the rules of the house we cannot even debate an identical resolution; we cannot refer to a debate which has taken place during the same session.
I have looked into the journals of the house in order to find whether a similar case has occurred under other circumstances and I have to go as far back as 1892 to find the last instance where a similar motion was presented to the house by Mr. Dalton McCarthy, who had a bill amending the Northwest Territories Act. That bill had been defeated on its second reading and he moved a motion similar to that moved by my hon. friend to-day. The Prime Minister at that time was Sir John Thompson, who opposed the motion, and I find at page 2483 of Hansard of 1892 these words of Sir John Thompson:
For one, I am not able to concur in the adoption of this motion, to-day. I think the house fully understood, when the question was put last night, that the principle of the bill was being voted on, and in relation to a public measure, as this is, it is a very unusual course to adopt such a motion.
I agree with that statement, and whatever may be our view as to the merits of the bill, I think that we should not vote to reinstate it on the order paper. I do not think that the arguments of my hon. friend are sufficiently strong to warrant the house taking the action he desires. My hon. friend said that the result of the vote was unsatisfactory, not because he was in favour of the bill, but because, I suppose, of the very small majority against the second reading. But I remember having taken part in divisions in this house where the majority was very small, and speaking for myself those were the finest votes in which I ever took part. Under parliamentary rule, a majority of one is just as good as a majority of ten, and if on this occasion we agree to this motion, what is to prevent us
from taking similar action on other measures at other times? After all, in parliamentary elections a candidate is elected sometimes by a majority of one. His opponent has the right to ask for a recount, but I have never heard it suggested that there should be a new election.
Another argument that my hon. friend used was that the vote came rather too soon, that it was not expected. It is difficult to satisfy those who do not want to be satisfied. I happened to read in the Toronto Saturday Night a few days ago an article by a writer stating that I had given instructions that the bill be talked out. This was of course untrue, as is shown by the statement of the mover of this resolution that the division came too early. I submit that if this motion carried, it would be bad parliamentary practice, and apart from that, it would be poor sportsmanship.

which has been invoked by the hon. member who moved this resolution is to my mind a very salutary and useful one. I was just going to say that although I differ with hon. members opposite on the merits of the bill which it is proposed to revive, I admire their pertinacity; but I appeal to their British sense of propriety in regard to parliamentary rules. This bill was brought up three years ago; it was brought up two years ago, and it was brought up last year. At one time it was defeated by a majority of thirty-one, this year it was defeated by a majority of one only. Cannot they foresee that they have a chance of winning by adopting the ordinary course of procedure? Do they not think that that would be the better way to proceed, if. what they propose is good for the country

which I do not admit- rather than damage their general cause in the eyes of a large section of the community, whether in Quebec or in Ontario, or in any part of the country, by endeavouring to force an issue now? They were defeated. I have been defeated. I remember occasions when I only had eight or ten members of the house with me as against the rest of the house; but the views that were expressed then were adopted ten or fifteen years later.
In view of all these things, it would be better to stick to the old and well established tradition which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has quoted. The tradition invoked by my hon. friend the member for Wetaskiwin is also a good one, and I would be the last member in this house to go against its maintenance. But, as everything unwritten and connected with the basic principles of parliamentary rule, it is based on common sense and reason. What is the reason of that tradition? That if a measure is defeated in the house by a snap vote, as it is usually called, on a day when most of the members do not expect the measure to come up, then it is quite proper for the house to give another chance to the movers of the measure to bring it up again. For example, suppose this measure had come up on a day when public orders are not the first order of business, and that the bill presented by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) had been defeated by a snap vote, opposed as I am to the bill, I would be the first to second the motion of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin; because I desire every member in this house, whether he holds the same view as I do, or whether he does not, to put his views before parliament and the country.
But was that the case here? The second reading of this bill came in its order. It came on the day that was designated for it. It has been said that the vote was small, and
that many members were absent from the house. Well, sir, comparing the total of that vote with the total of many votes in this house, on both public and private measures, you will find that it came well above the average. Should every measure be revived that has been defeated by a majority of one, or ten, in a house composed of about two-thirds of the members, or less than two-thirds, simply because the whole of the 215 members were not in their seats? It has been said that members who were absent should now have a chance to express their opinion. What about the members who were behind the curtains on both sides of the house? I counted at least twenty members going out from the house two minutes before the vote was called, going behind the curtains. Are we going to revive a motion in order to give these gentlemen time to make up their minds?
I appeal to parliamentary traditions and to my hon. friends on either side of the house, and ask them whether we are going to lay down the precedent that if some measure, whatever its merits may be, is defeated by a thin majority, we are going to bring it up again, to the detriment of all the measures propounded by other members of the house, which in their eyes must be of equal value to the measure under consideration, since they have placed their motions on the order .paper? Are we going to crowd out every member who has something to bring to the attention of .parliament in order to give some of the members a chance to re-hash twice in the same session a question which has been before the public for years, and which has been before both houses of this parliament for at least three years?

Nothing could more soundly

to t.he second reading of a measure, an amendment should be proposed that the measure should be read three months or six months hence. I recall looking into the reasons for the rule, and now we have the cause explained in* concrete form.
When the motion before the house is that a bill be now read a second time, the house by an adverse vote merely decides .that the measure shall not then be proceeded with, but if any hon. gentleman moves an amendment that all the words after "that" be struck out and that the bill be read this day three months or six months hence, then on the carrying of that amendment the measure would be killed for the session. The reason this measure may be again brought to the consideration of this bouse is that we have not yet negatived for the session the principle of the measure; the house merely declared the other evening that it was unwilling to accept the bill that night. The motion now before the house is that this bill shall be again brought before the house as you, Mr. Speaker, observed a moment ago.
I do deprecate very greatly a discussion of the merits of the bill at this time. It should not now 'be discussed. The motion now before the house is whether the hon, member shall have the opportunity again to place Bill No. 20 upon the order paper for consideration, regardless of its provisions. This bouse will now determine whether or not it desires that course of action to be taken-. I am Sony that I disagree in this instance with my hon. friend from St. LawrencenSt. George (Mr. -Caban) an-di wholly agree with the observations of the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon). It is so seldom I am in a position to agree with him that I direct attention to the fact. However, I am not now thinking of the provisions of the bill. I am dealing merely w'ith the constitutional right of this house to place upon .the order .paper for reconsideration a bill that it decided the other evening it was not disposed favourably to consider that night. If it is desired to deal finally with it this session, someone must move the three months' or six months' hoist or some other amendment to get it out of the way, provided always the house desires to deal with it in that way.
There is of course something to be said, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the larger question. While members from Ontario are peculiarly interested -in- -matters which affect Ontario, there is the national point of view that affects every member of this house, be he from the Yukon or from Prince Edward Island. We .must decide whether or not this house shall constitute itself a court, or dele-

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, March 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Dunning for committee of supply, the amendment thereto of Mr. Senn and the subamendment of Mr. Casgrain.
Mr. J. G. ROSS (Moose Jaw)):	Mr. Speaker, this question has already been discussed at considerable length in the house, but I wish to say a few words on it before a vote is taken. We have had figures presented which are reliable, to show that there is a larger production of dairy produce in Canada to-day than there has been in years past. There has been a much heavier consumption on account of a higher earning power of our people and also on account of a great deal of tourist traffic coming into our country. Prices have been shown to be higher in Canada than in other countries. This is natural when a country is on an import basis and products coming in must pay not only the world price but freight to the market in this country. It has been shown that the dairy industry throughout Canada has not been injured during the last few years.
One point I would like to make in connection with this amendment is that you cannot properly pick out one product of the farm and say that the country is going to the dogs because the production of that product rises or falls. Farming is a large business producing many different products and at one time it may be more profitable for the farmer to produce one product than another. For instance, if you take farming in western Canada and you start to gauge the prosperity of the country by the fact that the production of flax has fallen in the last few years, you would not have a proper comparison, because every one knows that flax is grown in the newer districts and on newer land, and as that part of the country becomes more settled, less flax is grown. Therefore you cannot pick out one product by which to judge the position of the industry of agriculture.
One of the arguments used by my hon. friends opposite is that because New Zealand and some other countries have a better climate, they can produce better and more cheaply than we can in Canada. In western Canada we used to do very little dairying. As a matter of fact, when western Canada was first settled, the idea was to go there 2410-454
and grow wheat. Everybody settled in western Canada originally as a farmer on a basis of growing wheat, but there has been a process of evolution in farming in the west, and to-day the lands that are more suitable for growing wheat are being used more and more for that purpose, while the lands unsuitable for wheat are being turned to mixed farming. In western Canada also, when we have a good crop of wheat-and wheat raising is an easier way of making money than dairying-our farmers grow wheat, but as soon as wheat crops fall off or prices fall off and the farmer must make his living, he turns to dairying, brings, in cows that have been under range or pasture raising calves, and starts to milk them in order to get his living throughout the winter. We have, as a matter of fact, in western Canada some of the best dairy herds that there are in the world. I would like to read a letter that I received from Mr. J. F. Singleton, Acting Commissioner of Dairy and Cold Storage. He says:
I am pleased to hand you herewith a copy of the extract from the report of the Dairy Commissioner for Saskatchewan for the year ending April, 1929, which extract I read to you this morning by telephone.
The extract is as follows:
Saskatchewan Cow Makes World Record
(From the report of the Dairy Commissioner for Saskatchewan for the year ended April, 1929.)
While not a part of the rvork of the Dairy branch, it is worthy of note that during the period under review a Saskatchewan owned cow completed a test which established a new world's record in butterfat production in the 3015 day test period for cows of all ages or breeds. The cow, a pure bred Holstein named Canary Korndyke Alcartra, was owned by B. H. Thomson of the Braeburn Farm, Boharm. This cow produced 1,080 pounds of butterfat in 305 days and dropped another calf just 378 days after the commencement of her test, thus coming well within the 400 day limit set for qualification for her record of performance certificate.
A significant feature of this record is that throughout the test period the cow stood in line with the other cows of the herd tied in a stanchion. She was milked three times a day, always by machine. She was, of course, fed very generously but almost entirely on home grown feeds. Her ration, in addition to pasture, consisted of ensilage, sweet clover hay, green oat sheaves, and a grain ration of two parts ground oats and one part bran to each hundred pounds of w'hich was added two pounds of bone meal and two pounds of salt.
Immediately on the announcement of this cow's record numerous inquiries were received by her owner as to whether she was for sale and one prospective purchaser made a definite cash offer of $10,000.00. A movement, started by the dairy producers of Moose Jaw District, resulted soon after in strong representations being made to the provincial government by the Saskatchewan Dairy Association and various

The cow mentioned in the letter of Mr. Singleton I believe has made another world's record this year for butter fat and milk production combined, having produced ,30,801 pounds of milk and 1,069 pounds of butter fat, which is equivalent to 1,301 pounds of butter. In this herd are many cattle which are only two year olds, and the lowest they have produced in the record of performance tests is 468 pounds per annum and up to 704 pounds. This will show you, Mr. Speaker, that although we are supposed to have a very rigorous climate in western Canada, and are not supposed to have the luscious pastures of green feed available in other parts of the world, still, under our conditions, and using as fodder only the feeds grown in western Canada, the cattle on the ordinary farm in Saskatchewan, in an ordinary kind of barn, standing in the ordinary milking herd, and milked by a milking machine, can break world records. In this connection I would point out that the average milk production for cows in the province of Ontario is 4,865 pounds per annum, the average butter fat production, 17C pounds, equivalent to 207 pounds of butter. The Canadian average for milking cows is 4,498 pounds of milk, and 157-43 pounds of butter fat, equivalent to 180-97 pounds of butter. In other words, of all the dairy cows in Canada, the average production of butter fat is 157 pounds per head.
My hon. friends opposite have been pointing out that the number of dairy cattle in this country has diminished in the last few years.

However, production has gone up. We have a very small amount of imports of dairy products to-day in comparison with the number of cattle that we have producing. The 3.200,000 cattle that we now have in Canada producing dairy products, if they produced an extra 10 pounds of butter fat per cow, would entirely wipe out our importations to-day. In the herd which I mentioned there are two cows that produce as much butter fat as twelve cows in the ordinary herd in the province of Ontario, so certainly it should not be very hard to increase the production per head of cattle in this country, and thereby wipe out any importations that we now have, if that is thought desirable. That increased production could be obtained without increasing the number of cattle at all. It is, of course, desirable to increase the production per unit, but the moment you put us on an export basis our butter prices must come down to the export price less the freight to market. When you do that, you reduce the price of butter in Canada to the export market some four or five or six cents a pound.
Last night, speaking to another motion, I said that I believed the real problem of agriculture in this country to-day had nothing whatever to do with tariffs.

product and what the consumer pays for it.
I believe that the Department of Agriculture is endeavouring to find ways and means of marketing our produce at a lower cost, and I think that we in this house should laud every effort that is made in that direction by the department or by any other agency, with a view to furthering the scientific marketing of farm produce, so that the farmer may get a larger return even though the price to the consumer is not raised, but on the contrary, may in some cases be lowered.
Trade in this world to-day has come down to a very, very eompetive basis. We cannot look for higher prices on so many of our products. It is all right for my hon. friend and others on his side of the house to move a resolution on the importation of eggs because he knows at this time of the year our hens start to lay. He knows that the Canadian hen will do her duty, she will lay more eggs at this time of the year than she has done for the last few weeks, and he goes to his farmer friends and says, "See how the imporation of eggs from the United States is lowering the price of our Canadian eggs." That is the reason why my hon. friend has advanced these arguments.
There is one phase of this debate that I have not heard mentioned a great deal, and that is inter-empire trade. We have been talking about cutting out importations of an empire product. I think that with the tremendous increase of production, not only of farm products, but also of manufactured products all over the world, the British Empire to-day is facing a crisis in trade probably as great as the political crisis of 1914. Our neighbour to the south of us has been set up by my hon. friend as an example of a high tariff country. True, there is a high tariff wall around the United States, but inside that high tariff wall amongst themselves they have the largest free trade area on the globe. If the British Empire is to carry on and prosper, then, provided we must have a tariff in this country, I think we should bend our efforts to lowering as far as possible all tariffs within the Empire, even though we keep up a tariff wall against the rest of the world. Lord Beaverbrook in the old country has been laughed at by some, and he also has been ridiculed in this country, but I think some of his ideas we might very well sift out and follow through to see if we cannot help trade within the empire as a whole. If the importations objected to happen to come from the United States, then they say the United States government is bullying this country into taking its products. This brings us to the season of 1928 which was a notable year in the history of the Canadian dairying industry. During 1928 the output of cheese was 6,547,000 pounds greater than in the previous year, and the premium paid for Canadian cheese in the British market was greater than ever before. More improvement in the quality of our dairy products was made in 1928 than in any other single year of our history. In our sister province of Quebec the improvement in the quality of the article was remarkable. There was a greater improvement made in that province that year than in the five previous
years. Yet the leader of the opposition as usual went back and forth all over this country preaching that the dairy industry in Canada was in a horrible condition. On the 25th of October he went to Montreal and told the people there that the dairy industry in this country -was being destroyed. Well, let us see whether it has been destroyed. The improvement in the quality of cheese brought an increased return of some $2,000,000 in that same year. Mr. Stephen, the secretary of the National Dairy Council, was in my room the other night and we discussed the whole question, as we have discussed it repeatedly, and before he left he could not but admit that the dairy industry in Canada was, comparatively speaking, in a most favourable condition. No man can say otherwise in the light of the information which is open to everyone. It is true that there was a decline in the amount of butter produced in 1928 from 271,000,000 pounds to 258,000,000 pounds, and a reduced value of some $2,339,000, but during the same year the value of the cheese produced increased by $4,983,661. There is a reason why there was a decline in the production of butter in our western provinces. It was largely because of the preoccupation of the farmers with their large wheat and other grain crops, and also on account of a shortage of suitable feed, as well as unfavourable climatic conditions. While I say this, it must be remembered that these are only two of the many lines of the Canadian dairy industry, and I shall deal with that later on. To sum up, there has been a remarkable recovery in dairying in the three western provinces during the past year, which according to the latest returns I have has led to an increased production of over 6,800,000 pounds of creamery butter alone. The entire production of butter in the three western provinces amounted in the same year to some 82,527,109 pounds.
Now I come to the year 1929. I have already shown that No. 1 pasteurized butteT at Montreal in 1927 commanded 4.72^ cents per pound higher than its value for export based on London prices; in 1928. 4.17i cents higher, and in 1929, 4.79 cents higher. These prices

Let us look for a moment at the whole dairy industry. Let us examine the economics of the whole situation regardless of party bias. It is not the cheese industry or the butter industry that makes up the whole daily industry of Canada. Analyze the facts that are open to us devoid of all party bias, and let the dhips fall where they may. If the situation shows no real development of the daily industry; if the faicts prove unfavourable to the record of the administration of this government, let them bear the brunt; their record is past and gone; it cannot be recalled, But in any case, 1st us be big enough for once to take a leaf from the life of the great Hugh Miller, the stone mason of Cromarty, Scotland, who, although deprived of the privilege of an early scholastic training, has written works that are to-day among the classics. Let us strive to take a leaf from his book, when in writing his Old Red Sandstone, his Footprints of the Creator, and more particularly, his Testimony of the Rocks, he said:
We pursue the search of the truth simply for its own sake, independently of the circumstances in which it may involve us or with what company it may make us acquainted.
If this analysis turns against the government, let the government rest under the lash. The horn, leader of the opposition knows full well that he is always preaching the doctrine of the home market. I am sorry he is not in the house, but I see my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) present. He, too, is always preaiehing the same doctrine. My hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) is allso always preaching that the home market is one of the great things for this government to look after. I quote from a paper read by Mr. J. F. Singleton, Chief of the division of dairy and cold storage of the federal Department of Agriculture, before the convention of the dairymen's association of eastern Ontario, at Kingston, on January 9, 1930. His analysis is so conclusive that I thank it ought to be placed on Hansard. He says:
In order to get a proper perspective of the condition of the dairying industry, it is necessary for us to consider total milk production and not that of any single commodity. Within certain limitations, rnilk flows into whatever channel is for the time being most profitable to the producer. Cities increase in population and must have more milk and cream for direct consumption and for the manufacture of ice cream. The source of supply is extended, and a price is paid which attracts milk from other 
outlets, such as from cheese factories and creameries. Changes in prices of cheese and butter, in relation to each other, cause diversion from one product to the other, and so it is necessary, in order to study the development of the dairying industry, to get back to total milk production or to the fat equivalent of the total milk production.

The fact is that our total returns for the dairy industry show an increase greater in 1929 than in any previous period of our history. Then there is another matter. Why the reduction in butter fat prices since January of this present year? That is a question which every dairyman has a right to ask and cream producers have a right to know-why butter fat prices must be reduced at this season of the year. I quote from the Canadian Countryman of February 22, 1930. This is the explanation given by the secretary of the Ontario Milk Producers' Association at the annual meeting of this association held in Toronto:
The situation confronting the condensery and milk powder branch of the industry at the present time is deserving of special mention. The prices the majority of the plants in this branch of dairying are able to pay producers for milk are controlled largely by the price of cream in the United States market. As you know, there has been a decided slump in cream prices there the past few months, owing to an oversupply of surplus milk. For the month of December the average price of 92 score butter in New York City was the lowest of any year for this month since 1916. January prices have not improved. On January 1, butter holdings in the United States totalled 81,837,000 pounds as compared with 43,580,000 pounds. This situation has had its effect on fluid milk prices also, in that country. These conditions in the United States market, coupled with the tariff increase on cream going into the United States, which came into effect last June, has had marked effect on prices for milk for condensery and milk powder purposes in Ontario during recent months, and is one of the primary causes of the rather unexpected increased supply of milk for city and town trade in this province.

Should we not see to it, in this present age when there is such a struggle for wealth, property and material possessions, that we do not neglect the higher things, the building up of the home and humanity? The home is the bulwark of the nation; history records the fact that it has been always so, and will con-
tinue to be so until the end of time. Pick up that old volume of the sacred law and what does it tell us? In the midst of all its wondrous words and admonitions to the human race it tells us that in mere wealth and outer splendor old Babylon had no rivals in ancient times but the fatal weakness of their people was that they put no real value upon true home life. As a consequence her gorgeous palaces and hanging gardens became the abode of selfishness and sensuality, with the result that we now read that over the spurious grandeur of that great city lie the sands of the desert and the calm of eternal night.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to say only two or three words on this amendment. We have been listening to so much recently on the subject of divorce that for one I can say that I am sick and tired of hearing about it. The object of this bill is not as the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. McMillan) would suggest, to make divorce easier; there is no hon. member in this house, and I hope there is no one outside the house, who wants in any way to impair the sanctity of the home or the stability of the family tie. The establishment of a divorce court in Ontario has nothing whatever to do with what the hon. gentleman has just said. We all think very highly of the home and I resent the imputation that it needs an amendment to a bill of this kind in order that we may be instructed in our attitude toward the sanctity of the home. We realize just as keenly, just as deeply and I think just as appreciatively the value of the home as do the hon. members who would seek by an amendment to take our minds away from the main purpose of this bill.
We have spent enough time in the house discussing this question; we have had it brought up by means of two or three bills, and I am sure that the people of this country expect us to get down to real business and not sit here perhaps for two weeks discussing family troubles in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
I realize that although I am elected for one proviin.ce, in a sense I represent the whole of Canada, as does every other hon. member, but in the province from which I come, we have a divorce court which has been in operation for some years. What is the result? The result is that divorce is not made easier;

Divodce Court jor Ontario
in fact it is much more difficult to obtain, in out province than it is through parliament. I was one of two or three members from the private bills committee who were asked to go to the Senate to see how the proceedings of the divorce committee of that house were conducted. I am not going to say that they are not fairly well conducted, but I submit that there is not the same regard to the taking of evidence and legal technicalities as would be the case before a competent judge and a competent court. Consequently those of us who have been supporting this bill are not advocating more divorces; we are not trying to lessen the sanctity of marriage; we are not trying to say anything against the building up and maintenance of the best homes we can have in this country. But we are trying to give to those who seek dissolution of the marriage tie, a better means of accomplishing it, one which will not increase the number of divorces but which in my judgment will on the contrary diminish them, because .they will be more difficult to obtain. I want to make it very emphatic that while I subscribe to the lofty sentiments contained in the amendment, I do not propose to be deterred from my duty by restricting myself to a consideration of those sentiments at the cost of defeating the real Object of the present bill. It is my intention, therefore, to vote against the amendment.

Which is equivalent to rescinding the treaty which was made with Australia and extended by order in council to New Zealand. I cannot subscribe to anything of that nature, something which treats our signed agreement as a scrap of paper. Such action will not commend itself to those in the country whom our hon. friends have sought to interest by means of this amendment.
The criticism of the agreement with New Zealand, particularly as it applies to the butter industry, has been based almost entirely upon the declining exports of butter. The hon. members opposite take that as their rule and guide in saying that the dairy industry is in a bad way and that the people engaged in that industry are suffering. I cannot agree with such an argument. The statistics which have been given in this debate, and the facts which were placed before the tariff advisory board at the time the application of the National Dairy Council was heard, should prove conclusively to any fair minded man that the dairy producers of Canada have been getting a better price for their milk, the raw material of that industry, than they were before the Australian treaty was negotiated. The Canadian market for dairy products has been better during the past year than the market in any other country in the world, and the same is true, with the possible exception of the United 
States, for the past two or three years. There has been a fair increase in production in this industry, and the different products give a better return to-day than they did before the treaty was negotiated. The quality of these products, particularly of butter, both for domestic and export markets, has been increased from year to year through the system of grading put into effect by our federal and provincial dairy branches.
The fact that our butter is of a high standard and that fresh butter can be so easily obtained has caused an increased home consumption of this product. We hear great wailing from our hon. friends opposite that the home market has not been protected, but this phase of the situation has been so handled that we find our home market for butter to be the best of any market in the world.
With such conditions obtaining we are forced to ask ourselves what our hon. friends opposite really mean by the amendment they have brought before the house. I believe it has a more far-reaching effect than is disclosed by the actual words. They ask that a treaty be negotiated upon fair and equitable terms, but some of the hon. members have gone further than that and have asked for a higher duty on butter. The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Price) read this afternoon a resolution passed by the farmers and dairymen in convention in the province of New Brunswick. I asked him if he subscribed to that resolution and he replied that he did. That resolution reads:
Whereas the National Dairy Council has made application for an increase in duties on butter in order to improve the dairy industry in Canada,
Therefore resolved that the convention go on record as fully supporting the National Dairy Council in their application.
What did the National Dairy Council ask for when it went before the tariff advisory board? I have in my hand the schedule which was presented to that board on January 14, and in that schedule they asked for a British preferential rate of four cents per pound, an intermediate rate of seven cents per pound, and a general rate of seven cents per pound, which is an increase over our present general tariff of three cents per pound. This would continue to give preference to those countries enjoying preferential rates, so that the motive of hon. members opposite would seem to be to obtain more protection for the dairy industry which supplies one of the main foods of the people of Canada. They ask for a tax on food. If it were necessary to follow up this argument, I could quote from other

Australian Treaty-Mr. Sinclair (Queens)
speeches made during the course of this debate to show that our hon. friends are asking for higher protection when they ask for the negotiation of a treaty with New Zealand.
Would higher protection help the dairy industry? Let us consider this question in a sane way. During the months of production our imports are lower, and when production decreases our imports increase. This has been so ever since the Australian treaty was negotiated, and it was so before that treaty was brought into effect. I submit that a higher duty placed upon butter coming into Canada simply would mean that the price of butter would be raised during the winter months with very little if any advantage to the producers of milk. Why do I say that? Because the only encouragement it would give would be to the man who wished to engage in speculation by storing butter bought at a low price in the summer season-and I think a careful perusal of the words of most of our hon. friends opposite will bear me out in that-by carrying that butter over until the winter months, and then by having the protection enabling him to extract more from the people of this country who have to buy butter than he would otherwise be able to do. It would give people who own cold storage warehouses or space in cold storage warehouses an opportunity to gamble to a greater extent with the food of the people and to increase the cost of living to the labouring classes at a time when, as hon. gentlemen opposite have told us on several occasions, we have a condition of seasonal unemployment as we are bound to have in Canada. It would make our labouring classes pay more for butter during the period of seasonal unemployment when they are not able to earn as much as they do in the busy season.

My hon. friend asks about the combines act. I have been informed there was another m-an connected with this, but I would not wish to mention

the name; a man who was very closely associated a short time ago with my hon. friend and who held a very important position in the Conservative party, is one of the close advisers of this corporation. It is financed by interests in the city of Toronto, and I do not think our hon. friends would accuse anyone other than themselves of being very greatly interested in that city.
Any increase in duty which is sought by this amendment would mean simply giving a greater stimulus ami opportunity to such large corporations as I have referred to, to get a wedge in between the milk producers and the consumers of the finished products of the dairies so that they may make a larger spread between the price paid to the producer and the cost to the consumer in the distribution of w-hat is one of our most wholesome and necessary food products. Any movement towards that end would be a mistake in this country. The position as it now obtains in the dairy business is sound. Our people are getting more for their product that they got formerly in comparison with world prices, and they will continue to do so. Our production is increasing. The quality of our product is second to none in the world. The dairy business of Canada was built up in its inception and has been brought to its present state largely by cooperative enterprises of the people who are producing milk in Canada. To give the producer the full benefit of his labour, and to give the consumer the article at as reasonable a price as possible, is a sound and sane method of building up a good industry. The spread between the price that the producer receives and the price that the consumer pays for butter as well as other dairy products has, I believe, kept within bounds, and anything that would tend to disrupt that condition would work to the distinct disadvantage of the producers in Canada.
There is another phase to the enlargement of the home market to which we should look, and which has done a good deal to change the texture of our population. The home consumption of butter has increased the production of butter. For the past two or three decades the trend of population as between urban and rural in Canada has been rapidly changing, until to-day I think it is fairly safe to say that the balance as between our urban and rural population is about fifty-fifty. I would not be surprised if the next decennial census should show that our urban population was larger than our rural. Certainly the urban population has increased very much in the last two or three decades. Parallel with that in-

Australian Treaty-Mr. Sinclair (Queens)
crease, there has been a corresponding increase in the production and export of manufactured products. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) told us in this debate a few nights ago that our exports of manufactured products had increased by sixty per cent. We know that the trade returns from year to year, particularly during the past decade, which includes the period since the war, have shown that Canada has gone ahead in increasing her manufactured .products m a very creditable way. That has brought about a change in the proportion between the rural and the urban population. Then, too, the adoption of the most modern methods of farming, and the introduction of machinery, which has manifested itself in a marked degree in western Canada in the last few years in the introduction of machinery for harvesting, has shown to us in eastern Canada that it may no longer be necessary to have the big harvester excursions that we had for many years past. Particularly has a change been brought about through the usse of machinery in central and eastern Canada, over a longer period and over a wider field of activity in mixed farming communities. In our own little province I think it is reasonably correct to say that we have a larger value of machinery to the acre than any other province in Canada. Under those conditions our production has been not only kept up but increased, v'hile our rural population at the same time has been decreasing compared with the urban population. This has caused a change in all lines of agricultural activity.
When we approach a matter of this kind dealing with one particular branch of the dairy industry, we must give full consideration to every other line of the dairy business, as well as to the relation of the dairy business to other branches of agriculture. In eastern Canada the dairy business has been the most profitable of our mixed farming operations. In our little province of Prince Edward Island, as well as in some of the agricultural sections of New Brunswick, our people have turned a little to the raising of a cash crop in the form of potatoes, but I do not think that that has been done to the neglect of the dairy industry. I am sure that the future will show that our farmers have not lost sight of the value of the dairy industry, and that any diminution in the number of cows kept or the amount of milk produced during the past year has been due largely to seasonal conditions. Any diminuation that has been caused in a few cases by farmers diverging into cash crops will be only temporary. Our people in the years to come will develop the dairy business to a greater degree than ever before.
There is another feature of the amendment of hon. gentlemen opposite which would operate against the interests of Canada generally. If the duty on butter and dairy products were increased, as hon. gentlemen opposite desire, the family budget of the workingman in Canada would be increased. Some of our labouring population find themselves at certain seasons of the year without work, and we must always expect, on account of our climatic conditions, to have seasonal unemployment. Now if we are going to increase the cost of the food of these people and make their living dearer, they will demand higher wages from their employers, and in that way raise the standard of living in Canada and put us at a disadvantage Rather than raise the price by artificial means, that will be of no direct benefit to the producer, it would be much better to take steps, governmental, if you will, to make it possible for our dairy farmers to obtain the cheaper concentrates and cheaper feeds which it is necessary for almost even-dairy farmer to buy. I do not mean to advocate the buying of dairy feeds by the farmer, except to supplement the feeds he raises on his farm, but it is recognized in the maritime provinces particularly that our dairy farmers as well as those engaged in other side lines, such as poultry and hogs, are paving too much for the feeds that it is necessary for them to buy to balance the rations for the stock which they raise on their farms. We can do more for the dairy industry, I submit, if we take steps to make available to our dairy farmers at as low a price as possible the feeds that are necessary, and thus reduce the cost of production.

When the question was asked by the leader of the opposition I was referring, Mr. Speaker, to the detrimental effects that any action tending to raise the cost of living would bring about in this country. I have in my hand an article, published in yesterday's Citizen, headed Australian Industry to Canada, copied from the Canadian Co-operator. It is as follows:
It is a fact well known to economists that the beneficiaries of a protectionist policy derive their advantage from the excessive prices they are allowed, through the operation of tariff laws, to charge the home consumers. A county with a high protective tariff is, however, at a great disadvantage when it has to compete in foreign markets with other countries having a free-trade or low-tariff policy. Evidence of this fact is to be found in the following, taken from the International News Service (Economic

Section) of the International Co-operative Alliance:	"An interesting comment on
Australian high protectionist policy is provided by the news that the Sunshine Harvester Works near Melbourne have concluded an agreement with the Waterloo Manufacturing Company of Ontario, Canada. The latter company will now undertake to manufacture the former's patent threshing machine, which has been very successful in Australia, and is finding increasing favour in North America and elsewhere. Mr. Speaker, I wish to discuss briefly the subject at present under consideration, because the amendment, to my mind, does not conform with the interests of the people at large. For the last few months our Conservative friends have been scouring the rural districts of Quebec, trying to convince the farming classes that they are suffering from the effects of the order in council

Australian Treaty-Mr. Robitaille
which grants to New Zealand the same advantages afforded to Australia. They do not stop at that. They distribute profusely pamphlets in which the King Government is charged with ruining the farming classes. However, our good farmers are quite on their guard. I want to draw the attention of the house to this unfair propaganda which is contrary to the country's interest. What are the charges brought against the Liberal policy in connection with the concessions which were granted to New Zealand? It is stated that we imported 35,000,000 pounds of butter in 1929. I want to point out that, in his speech, the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) contends that the Ontario factories were forced to purchase butter in order to fill their orders. If we look up the statistics on the subject we find that we have only exported
8764,000	worth of butter, while we imported
35,000,000 pounds from New Zealand. Yet, what is the price of butter? Last summer, in the Montreal district, we paid for butter 42 cents per pound, and in the autumn 45 cents. At present we are paying 45 cents per pound- I refer to prices at butter factories. Notwithstanding the importation of 35,000,000 pounds of butter, prices have not come down. Yet the butter was consumed. We have none left, we are not exporting any. What would have happened if the policy of our opponents had prevailed? Where would we have got butter, and what would have been the price? We must not only consider the producers, we must also think of the consumers who are far more numerous. Whether you increase the price of butter or of any other article, it is always the consumer who pays.
Our opponents are prone to imitate the United States or to cite them as an example. For the last two yeans, the United. States have advocated a protective tariff for their farming classes. What are the means resorted to by the United States government so as to give these classes a measure of protection? For how many months past have these gentlemen been endeavouring to protect the farmers? What has been the result? They apparently granted them a certain protection; however, on the other hand they increased the tariff on other products than those of the farm. So much so, that a United States senator made the remark that farmers, in return for a few favour's, would have, for instance, to pay yearly-owing to the increase in customs duties-on cement, about $53,000,000 more; on sugar, about $32,000,000; on oil and its byproducts, about $904,000,000, and on lumber
about $50,000,000 more. Will this give protection to farmers? The small benefit which they will derive from protection, will soon be absorbed by the increase in duties that they will have to pay on other products. Now, sir, why do we consume so much butter? First, it was pointed out that we sold about 100,000 milch cows to the United States, and those who disposed of them are far from having suffered from such a sale, since they obtained a price varying from $150 to $300. And if, because of this, the herds have decreased, we must not also lose sight of the fact that they have decreased because they failed to pass the tuberculine test. Yet, had we not been fortunate enough to import butter on favourable terms from New Zealand, we certainly would have run short of it; then, our working classes and the consumer as a whole would have paid exorbitant prices. One must not think that by placing a tariff on butter we shall induce the farmer to increase his herd and that he may expect the necessary farm hands to raise them profitably. There are certainly other means. At all events, the market is not over crowded. The farmeT can easily increase his herd without fear of any overproduction of dairy products. He will certainly find all the markets necessary, since he sells, at present, his milk and cream not only in this country but also in the United States.
Therefore, it is not by increasing the duties to the extent of preventing the importation of these products that the farmer will increase his wealth. The idea of giving preference to the home market has for a long time been advocated. Are we not encouraging such a market when we absorb in this country the entire production of our dairy industry? Indeed, statistics prove that we do not export these products or very little.
Considering these faicts, I think that the amendment has been introduced with a political purpose only, and that it is of too sweeping a character. The treaty of 1925 was passed having regard to the prevailing conditions of that time. It might not, therefore, be out of place if certain changes were made in keeping with the present time. However, it will always be necessary to conform with the treaty enacted between the two dominions; we must also show some regard for the convention, that is, give the six months' notice as agreed, and not act too hastily. I submit that the subamendment should be accepted by the house in preference to the amendment, and for the reasons given I shall support the subamendment.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have before the house the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) that this house resolve itself into committee of supply. We have also an amendment and a subamendment. It is only in recent years, Mr. Speaker, that members of this house have been permitted, under the rules, to move a subamendment when the house resolves itself either into committee of supply or into committee of ways and means. Some two or three years ago a special committee was appointed for the purpose of revising the rules, and one of the suggestions made by that committee and adopted by the house was to the effect that a subamendment be permitted when the house resolved itself into committee of ways and means and committee of supply. It is quite possible that the reason the committee made the suggestion was that we no longer have the two party system in the house, and certain groups were not in a position under the former rules to express their views on important questions owing to the fact that the moving of only one amendment was permitted. On this occasion we had the usual motion by the Minister of Finance, then we had the amendment moved by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn), and the subamendment, moved by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain). The subamendment precluded hon. members in this house from expressing their opinion on this very important question. We do not deny that -the government has the right to use the subamendment process just as well as we have. We believe the amendment to the rules-to which I have referred -is in the interest, of all parties and groups in this house, but. on this occasion the group in this corner has not had the opportunity, as I have said, of moving a subamendment, and neither the amendment nor the subamendment expresses our views. Therefore we have decided. Mr. Speaker, not to take any part in the vote, either on the subamendment or on the amendment. We do not propose to vote either for or against either of the two motions, but will take an opportunity later of laying before the house our viewpoint on this important matter.

this is not a formal motion in any sense. It far transcends anything that is formal because the government itself is the author of its own motion, through the chief whip. I would entirely agree if this were an ordinary case in which the two precedents cited by my hon. friend were applicable, the one where Sir Leonard Tilley moved the house into committee of supply and the government accepted an amendment that was moved by one of the supporters. The same thing occurred in 1900, when the question came up on Mr. Russell's amendment to go into supply. The government accepted that amendment. But here the amendment has not been accepted by the government. It has been defeated by the government by a subamendment interposed by the action of the government itself, and that subamendimemt has now become an amendment to the motion. That is the distinction. The question that you have now put to the house is: Shall the motion as amended be adopted? That motion as amended is the original motion to go into supply, plus the amendment moved as want of confidence in the government, but which the government itself has replaced by a subamendment which now becomes an amendment to a motion to go into supply, which motion with the amendment they now say we propose, not to drop, but to ask to have carried. So what has happened is that this government's motion to go into supply has been carried as amended. I submit, on the very same principle on which the hon. member for Wetaskdwin (Mr. Irvine) moved his motion with respect to a private bill to-day, that this is no longer a formal motion. The committee .of supply is now destroyed because the government has passed a subamendment to the amendment to the motion for going into supply. That subamemdment having been accepted by the government and carried, they are faced with a new condition, new under the practice and recent rules of this house. The government must, make a motion to go into supply which is n.ot a formal motion. As was pointed out by my hon. friend a moment ago, the last citation given by you, sir, referred to a future day. It would be quite competent, for the government to move that this house go into supply to-morrow; I agree as to that.

Under those circumstances, Mr. Speaker, we were debarred from using the new rule. Of course, we do not object to the government making use of the new rule for the purpose for which they invoked it, although primarily the rule was brought into existence to give members of the third party an opportunity of expressing themselves.
The negotiations for the Australian treaty were initiated by the late Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). I believe when he was Minister of Trade and Commerce he visited Australia and had certain conversations with the Australian government, and on his return to Canada he continued the negotiations. Certain proposals were made in the first instance, which later were abandoned, and the negotiations were continued by representatives of the Canadian government going to Australia. Finally a second agreement was entered into which formed the basis of the treaty.
Now, we claim that the Australian treaty was negotiated primarily for the purpose of providing markets for our manufactured goods; that was the prime purpose of the treaty. Very little consideration, in fact no 
consideration at all, was given to the possibilities of exporting agricultural and other products of this country to the Australian market. Therefore, we take objection, first of all, to the manner in which the treaty was negotiated, and secondly, to the incidence of the treaty itself. We object very strongly, for certain reasons which I will give later, Mr. Speaker, but in view of the fact that it is eleven o'clock, I shall resume my remarks on the next occasion when this motion is before the house.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
